title: Colorectal Cancer Screening with Optical Coherence Tomography
text:
In this grant, we will overcome the high cost and inefficacies of colonoscopy for cancer screening by developing
and validating new in vivo microscopic imaging technologies for detecting and treating cancer precursors called
colorectal adenomas. Successful completion of this research will significantly improve colorectal cancer
screening by enabling higher adenoma detection rates, and by providing a less invasive screening tool that can
automatically detect and treat adenomas at the point of care without requiring sedation.

title: The Effect of Myopia on Retinal Ganglion Cells, Astrocytes and Vasculature, and its Relationsip to Glaucoma Susceptibility
text:
Myopia and glaucoma pose significant public health concerns - half the world’s population is
projected to be myopic by 2050 and glaucoma is estimated to affect more than 120 million people
worldwide by 2040, which in turn will increase the global prevalence of myopic glaucoma
significantly. Evidence shows that myopic patients are at higher risk of glaucomatous
degeneration, however the mechanisms behind the myopia-glaucoma association remain
unknown. The proposed research aims to identify the effect of myopia on three retinal
neurovascular cell types crucial for ganglion cell survival, and their relationship with glaucoma
susceptibility, in a novel non-human primate model of myopia that will be subsequently induced
with glaucoma.

title: Reprogramming cell-fate decisions through predictive modeling and synthetic biology
text:
Synthetic biology holds the promise of transforming the development of diagnostic and treatment strategies for
various diseases. This project applies synthetic biology approaches to reprogram fate decisions toward
progressive cellular deterioration, a key factor in many diseases, such as cancers, diabetes, and
neurodegenerative diseases. Key insights obtained from this project will define foundations for chemical or gene-
based strategies to treating diseases related to progressive cellular deterioration.

title: Growth in Medicare Advantage Enrollment and its Implications for Cancer Care Quality
text:
Enrollment in Medicare Advantage (MA)—private health plans which administer Medicare benefits—has rapidly
grown among Medicare beneficiaries with cancer, yet research examining its impact on the quality of cancer
care is limited. Using a large, representative sample of Medicare beneficiaries in cancer registries and linked
Medicare data, this project will investigate the quality of cancer care in MA and Traditional Medicare (TM) and
the effect of selective provider networks (a key feature of MA benefit design) on care quality. The project will
also include a qualitative component to examine the drivers of exclusions of advanced cancer centers in MA
networks, helping to identify opportunities for optimizing MA networks and improving cancer care delivery in
Medicare.

title: Frontal-thalamo-cerebellar circuitry of attention deficit via imaging-genetic-environmental analyses
text:
Attention deficit is one of the most common developmental problems in the general population. Focusing on the frontal,
thalamus and cerebellum of the brain, this study investigates how brain structural and functional features underlie the
attention deficit and finds genetic factors regulating these brain attributes. Finally, this study will build a prediction model
for the attention deficit using brain attributes together with genetic and environmental factors.

title: Uncover the role of H3.3-G343R mutation in shaping the DNA damage response, anti-tumor immunity and mechanisms of resistance in glioma.
text:
Pediatric high-grade gliomas (pHGGs) are one of the most common and aggressive forms of
brain cancer, with a median survival of 9-15 months. We aim to study a subtype of pHGG which
harbors H3.3-G34R, ATRX and TP53 inactivating mutations. Our goal is to assess the molecular
mechanisms by which H3.3-G34R impacts the biology of pHGGs, influence the tumor immune
microenvironment and the response to therapeutics, including immune-mediated mechanisms.

title: Resource of zebrafish models of human diseases
text:
This project will generate a resource of rigorously validated, reproducible, and translatable animal disease-
models. A bioinformatics pipeline will be used to analyze and prioritize sequence variants of unknown
significance from patients for study. Humanized zebrafish models of the patient variants will be generated,
validated, and deposited at the NIH-funded Zebrafish International Resource Center.

title: Novel expression of MHC class II on DRG neurons and its role in promoting antinociceptive CD4+ T cells in females during chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy
text:
Chemotherapeutic agents are often dose limiting due to the emergence of a debilitating and painful
neuropathy, posing a major challenge to the successful treatment of cancer. Post-menopausal breast and
ovarian cancer patients are more at risk for developing paclitaxel-induced peripheral neuropathy.
Characterizing neuron-immune communication and enhancing endogenous analgesic CD4+ T cells may
provide a means for prophylactic and therapeutic intervention.

title: Predoctoral Training Program in Biological Data Science at Brown University
text:
(3 sentences).
A successful research career studying the biological systems and human diseases also involves the analysis of
complex and multi-scale datasets; for example, many biomedical studies now routinely integrate -omic and cel-
lular data with population-level covariates and digitized assessments of traits of interest. This predoctoral training
program at Brown University will yield multiple cohorts of researchers who are uniquely interdisciplinary— work-
ing at the interface of biomedical data generation and data science research — via didactic, research, and pro-
fessional development opportunities that foster scientific “dual citizenship” at the faculty and student levels. This
training program aligns with the NIGMS mission by training a new generation of Biological Data Scientists, as-
suring the vitality and continued productivity of basic research as biological datasets expand in size, scale, and
complexity.

title: Resolution Enhancement and Contrast Harmonization for MR Neuroimaging
text:
The project will develop and evaluate software to improve the resolution and correct the tissue contrast of
magnetic resonance brain images using advanced postprocessing methods. This new approach will permit
improved quantification of clinical brain images using automatic medical image analysis methods.

title: Methodological Training for Social and Behavioral Research in Cancer Control
text:
Cancer is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality. Social and behavioral factors influence cancer risk and
preventive behaviors, screening, incidence, treatment utilization, and survivorship. This program will provide
cutting-edge predoctoral methodological training to translate fundamental knowledge about social and
behavioral science into innovative interventions and policies for cancer prevention and control.

title: Project 3 - Mechanisms of extra- and intra-cellular calcification
text: PROJECT 3 SUMMARY Mechanisms of extra- and intra-cellular calcification. Recent findings from our laboratory showed that extracellular calcification is an integral part of the hallmark lesions of age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Calcified deposits rich in the calcium phosphate mineral hydroxyapatite (HAP) accumulate in the space under the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) in the back of the eye, where nutrient uptake and clearance of unwanted material usually are exchanged between the blood circulation and the RPE cells. Inhibition of this exchange process can lead to rapid progression to an end-stage disease characterized by irreversible visual loss. Apart from AMD, sub-RPE deposit formation is also associated with other diseases such as Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Based on recent findings, we proposed a new model for sub-RPE deposit initiation and growth where calcification plays a pivotal role. We know from clinical and basic science studies that calcification, and the associated interactions with proteins and lipids, have a negative effect on disease progression. We also learned that understanding how different mineralization forms contribute to diseases is critical. However, we do not yet know how calcification occurs and what intra- and extracellular molecules and pathways contribute to mineral deposition in the sub-RPE space. This project will study the cellular and systemic contributors to extracellular mislocalized (ectopic) calcification using a cellular model system we developed to study the initiation and progression of the mineral-laden sub-RPE deposits. We will also develop a significantly improved, new 3D microfluidic cell model to study calcification, as sub-RPE deposit formation, development and progression of AMD and AD are linked to the choroidal endothelium and its degeneration. The results will be validated using human postmortem eye tissues from patients with AMD and AD. The validation and the experimental plan using the 2D and 3D cell culture systems will provide a robust foundation for developing new intervention strategies centered on the calcification of the sub-RPE deposits. Apart from AMD and AD, these treatment strategies will also be applicable for other diseases in which sub-RPE deposits play a role.

title: Cell Fate Decisions in Epithelial Stem Cell Lineages
text:
The proposed research will provide a foundation for understanding how cell fate decisions are controlled within
an epithelial stem cell lineage. Epithelial stem cells are central to both normal homeostasis and the
progression of diseases such as cancer, so understanding how they are regulated their native, in vivo contexts
is important for the development of new diagnostics and therapeutics. The proposed project will also
contribute to the NIH mission to foster fundamental creative discoveries by investigating new and poorly
understood topics such as stem cell niche competition and the role of pH dynamics in cell fate decisions.

title: Behavioral-Biomedical Interface: Translational and Prevention Sciences Training
text:
This institutional training grant supports the University of South Carolina Behavioral-Biomedical
Interface Program, which helps to prepare future behavioral scientists to be better equipped to
address the complex challenges inherent in health research. Pre-doctoral trainees in public
health and psychology acquire important biological and biomedical foundations in concert with
their behavioral science disciplinary training. This program adds scientists to the workforce who
are able to more effectively translate research into understanding, preventing, and treating
health disorders of major societal import.

title: Disease Pathogenesis and Modification for CaV1.1-Associated Hypokalemic Periodic Paralysis
text:
Hypokalemic periodic paralysis (HypoPP) is a rare inherited disorder of skeletal muscle in which
recurrent episodes of severe weakness, and the risk of progressive weakness with loss of
ambulation, are caused by mutations of either calcium channel or sodium channel genes.
Contemporary management of symptoms, with lifestyle changes or empirical usage of carbonic
anhydrase inhibitors, is inadequate with diminished quality of life and no effective means to
prevent late-onset permanent muscle weakness. This project builds upon the insights from our
30 years of investigating pathomechanisms of HypoPP to the rational design and preclinical
testing of new pharmacologic approaches to mitigate acute attacks and of gene therapies for a
more durable management that may also prevent late onset myopathic weakness.

title: Viral and host determinants of orthobunyavirus entry.
text:
La Crosse virus is the leading cause of arboviral encephalitis in American pediatric populations and can result
in life-long neurological complications. This work will study the molecular interactions between LACV and a newly
discovered host factor JAG2 and the functional consequences of these interactions on LACV infection. This
foundational knowledge of viral entry mechanisms is essential for development of novel medical
countermeasures.

title: WISDOM: A platform to optimize subtype-specific screening and prevention
text:
OVERALL: NARRATIVE
The WISDOM Study, opened in 2016, is the first large clinical trial of a new, personalized approach to breast
cancer screening in which women receive individualized screening recommendations based on their personal
risk for breast cancer. While our initial efforts were focused on showing that personalized screening was as
safe, less morbid, preferred and more likely to result in uptake of preventive strategies in comparison to annual
screening, we will now focus on using advances in polygenic risk models and mammographic AI to improve our
ability to predict risk for developing fast or slow growing breast cancer subtypes, and tailoring screening and
prevention strategies accordingly. Four closely integrated projects will enable us to work toward the goal of a
personalized breast cancer screening program that is more effective and efficient, and more likely to help find
serious breast cancers early, when they are more likely to be treated successfully, and decrease the incidence
of slow growing cancers.

title: Synthesis, secretion and assembly of extracellular complex carbohydrates in Gram-negative bacteria
text:
Extracellular polysaccharides are produced by many organisms and perform a plethora
of essential functions in life. The polymers can also protect many pathogens, thereby
supporting survival inside the host. Our research seeks to unravel how extracellular
polysaccharides are synthesized and deposited on the cell surface.

title: Mechanistic Dissection of Lamina Associated Domain Reorganization in Fibrosis
text:
Fibrosis is a major contributor to morbidity and mortality in aging populations as it contributes to chronic diseases
in multiple tissues, such as the heart, lung, and skin. By uncovering how nuclear genome organization regulates
fibroblast activation, a central driver of fibrosis, this work identifies upstream mechanisms that could be targeted
to prevent or reverse pathological tissue remodeling. Understanding and manipulating these chromatin-based
pathways has the potential to enable new therapeutic strategies for a broad range of fibrotic diseases that
currently lack effective treatments.

title: Structure and function of KATP channels
text:
ATP-sensitive potassium (KATP) channels regulate membrane excitability according to the energetic state of a
cell and are important for many physiological functions. KATP channel dysfunction underlies several devastating
human diseases. The goal of this project is to understand the structural mechanisms governing the activity of
various KATP channel subtypes found in different tissues and use the knowledge to design better drugs to treat
diseases caused by channel dysfunction.
